visuals.concept: Relationship between environmental lapse rate (ELR), dry adiabatic lapse rate (DALR) and saturated adiabatic lapse rate (SALR), and how their relative position determines absolute/conditional/absolute stability.

source.notes: Embedded born-digital raster extracted directly from the page at native resolution (1398x1665).

visuals.mapping_reason: The chart explicitly labels DALR = 3°C/1000ft (33, 646), the ELR>DALR absolutely-unstable region (676, 1495), and the DALR<ELR>SALR conditionally-unstable region defined by dry-vs-saturated air (1475). Questions about visibility/cloud characteristics of stable/unstable air (52, 55, 624) were left unmapped since this chart shows lapse-rate regions, not visibility outcomes; their old AI-generated placeholder image was removed rather than force-fit to a weak match.

visuals.concept: The Foehn effect: moist air forced up the windward slope cools, condenses and rains out, then descends the lee slope as dry air that warms at the (faster) dry adiabatic lapse rate, producing a warm, dry downslope wind.

visuals.concept: The Coriolis effect: an air parcel's path curving to the left (Southern Hemisphere) as pressure-gradient force and Coriolis force interact.

visuals.concept: Buys Ballot's Law: with the geostrophic wind blowing left across a low-over-high pressure gradient, an observer with their back to the wind has low pressure on their right in the Southern Hemisphere.

source.figure: Figure 4.51, The Creation of Geostrophic Wind
source.notes: Embedded born-digital raster extracted directly from the page. This is the exact figure the book's text cross-references when explaining Buys Ballot's Law for the Southern Hemisphere.

visuals.mapping_reason: With low pressure north and high pressure south and the geostrophic wind blowing west (left), an observer facing downwind (west) has north - and therefore the low - on their right, matching the question's answer exactly.

visuals.concept: Surface friction reduces the Coriolis force relative to the pressure-gradient force, so the near-surface wind veers (turns clockwise) away from the geostrophic direction toward the low pressure.

source.notes: Embedded born-digital raster extracted directly from the page. Explicitly labelled 'Ageostrophic Wind... veers towards the low pressure zone', a clockwise turn from the pure geostrophic (westward) direction.

visuals.mapping_reason: Question 719 asks what veering means (a clockwise directional change); this figure is the book's own diagram of veering caused by surface friction. Question 720 (backing, anticlockwise) was left unmapped since this figure shows only the clockwise case.
